title: Attacking AERO the Pedantic Way
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman takes apart a new anonymous critique of the Australian Education Research Organisation (AERO), published by a self-styled 'Australian Centre for the Public Understanding of Education' (ACPUE) that claims to have found widespread citation problems in an AERO evidence report. Ashman's method is to walk through ACPUE's own scoring table and show that its 'does not match' verdicts are frequently generated by an uncharitable, hyper-literal reading standard rather than genuine citation error: a claim supported by three references gets flagged if any one reference does not independently cover the entire claim, even when the other two clearly do. He gives several worked examples, including a First Nations education claim and a claim about high expectations and belonging, where ACPUE's own data shows the core references match but the site still reports the citation as failing on a technicality, and one case where ACPUE's stated reasoning appears to be a garbled non-sequitur. Ashman also flags that ACPUE cannot document who runs the site, that its headline statistics (47% of claims, 42% of citation checks) don't reconcile with the numbers in its own table, and that its report covers only one AERO publication while being framed as a verdict on AERO's 'evidence claims' generally. He closes by noting the irony of a pedantic citation-accuracy campaign arriving just as Cambridge's education faculty is dealing with a genuine plagiarism scandal, and warns ACPUE that its own anonymous work is now fair game for the same scrutiny it applied to AERO.
points: Ashman's core critique is methodological: ACPUE marks a claim's citation as 'does not match' if any single supporting reference (among several) fails a strict, standalone test, even when the other references clearly support the claim — a standard he calls uncharitable rather than rigorous.

He shows ACPUE's own headline statistics (47% of claims, 42% of citation checks 'do not match') don't reconcile with the underlying table, which shows 40.7% for the citation-check figure, and the site provides no way to verify the 'misused references' statistic at all.

Worked examples (the First Nations education claim, the high-expectations-and-belonging claim) show ACPUE flagging references as mismatches over definitional disagreements — e.g. whether 'guided independence' equals 'guided, structured inquiry' — rather than actual citation errors.

ACPUE publishes with no listed CEO, team, or board, and Ashman notes it could be a single author using an AI tool, which he treats as relevant to how much authority its citation-accuracy verdicts should carry.

Ashman contrasts ACPUE's pedantic treatment of AERO's citations with the contemporaneous, genuinely large-scale citation scandal at Cambridge's education faculty, suggesting the energy directed at AERO is disproportionate to the underlying problem.
quotes: This is uncharitable because the AERO authors have supported the claim with the other two papers and Jones may only be relevant to a part of it.

Seriously? And what, exactly, are we arguing about here? Is there a counterclaim that building and sustaining high expectations does not foster positive relationships that needs to be addressed, despite the other supporting references?
It is reasonable to have different views on such definitions, but this is a difference of opinion and not an example of a citation error.
They claim 47% of claims do not match, 42% of citation checks do not match and 67% of references are misused at least once. I cannot reverse-engineer these figures.

There is an irony in this exercise coming to light in the wake of Cambridge University — and its education faculty — being consumed by an alleged plagiarism scandal, with attempts by some in academia to wave away genuine, large-scale citation irregularities.
It could be one dude prompting Claude or it could be a team of disgruntled and marginalised education lecturers. We don't know.

I am dying to know who they are because they have now given me licence to subject their own work to a similar, if more robust, citation analysis, something I would relish but would otherwise avoid out of politeness.
